Instructions for submitting Observer reports 
Introduction 
This document provides the reporting template and instructions for Observers to report 
during the 2023 - 2025 Norwegian Chairship of the Arctic Council. 

The deadline for submission is 1 December 2024. 
 

Role of Observers 
The role and responsibilities of Observers, as well as criteria for admission to the Arctic 
Council, can be found in the “Arctic Council Rules of Procedure” (Annex 2) and the 
“Observer Manual for Subsidiary Bodies.” 

The primary role of Observers is to observe the work of the Arctic Council. Observers 
contribute to the Arctic Council primarily through engagement at the level of Working 
Groups, Task Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Observers are invited to the meetings and 
other activities of the Arctic Council unless the Senior Arctic Officials decide otherwise. 
Observers may also propose projects through an Arctic State or a Permanent Participant. 

Report submission 
Observer reports should include the relevant information described below and in the 
template. 

(a) A description of the Observer’s contributions to the work of the Arctic Council since 
the time of the Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years, with 
special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies through project participation 
and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent Participants; 

(b) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s future plans to contribute to the work of 
the Arctic Council, with special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies 
through project participation and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent 
Participants; and, 

(c) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s contributions to other aspects of the 
Arctic Council and its goals not covered in the previous sections since the time of the 
Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years. 

 

Observer reports should be submitted electronically to the Arctic Council Secretariat via 
email: acs@arctic-council.org not later than 1 December 2024. Please bear in mind while 
preparing your report that all Observer reports will be published online in the Observer 
section of the Arctic Council online Library (OAR) following the Chairship transition. 

If an Observer fails to submit a report, the Arctic Council will consider this to mean that the 
Observer is no longer interested in maintaining its status as an accredited Observer to 
the Arctic Council.

1. Advocacy and Strategic engagements in the domain of polar and cryosphere through the WMO 
Executive Council Panel on Polar and High Mountain Observations, Research, and Services 
(PHORS) 

The 19th World Meteorological Congress has renewed the focus of WMO on polar regions and the 
cryosphere by adopting the resolution on priorities to address the global and regional impacts of 
changes in the cryosphere. The WMO Executive Council (EC) has renewed the mandate of the Panel on 
Polar and High Mountain Observations, Research, and Services (PHORS), with the role of supporting 
effective collaborations with partners organizations and stakeholders outside of WMO, including the 
Arctic Council and its Working Groups. The focus of PHORS activities is on polar and high mountain 
regions and, globally, on vulnerable regions where the irreversible changes in snow, glaciers, 
permafrost and seasonally frozen ground, icesheets, sea-ice, and freshwater and sea ice, and ice 
sheets amplify the impacts of climate change. The panel is co-chaired by the Permanent 
Representative of Norway with WMO, Dr Roar Skålin and that of New Zealand, Mr Stephen Hunt. 

On 12 February 2024, PHORS organized in Oslo a high-level event on Cryosphere: from science to 
policy to action with the participation of officials from the Norwegian Government, the Arctic Council 
Secretariat, and the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme (AMAP). The event was part of the 
13th session of PHORS, hosted by the Norwegian Meteorological Institute and, also, benefiting from 
the financial support of Environment and Climate Change Canada. 

2. Engagements at programme level 

2.1 Arctic Regional Climate Centre network 

Under the leadership of WMO and coordination by PHORS, an Arctic Regional Climate Centre Network 
(ArcRCC-Network) has been established to meet the Arctic adaptation and decision-making needs. 
ArcRCC-Network is based on the WMO RCC concept with direct contributions from all the Arctic 
Council member countries through a mutually agreed structure consisting of three sub-regional 
geographical nodes, namely, (i) North America, (ii) Northern Europe and Greenland and (iii) Eurasia 
Nodes. The users of climate information of the ArcRCC are engaged via Arctic Climate Forums (ACF) – 
as regional user engagement platforms; this includes AMAP, which has been engaged actively in the 
definition of requirements and the dissemination of results. ArcRCC-Network will also provide 
important input to the Early Warnings for All (EW4All) initiative through Climate Watch Advisories. 

Upon the successful completion of demonstration phase, ArcRCC-Network was designated as a WMO 
RCC in June 2024. Its contributions are well aligned with the goals of AMAP and AMAP Climate Expert 
Group. All relevant information and products are freely available accessible through a 
https://www.arctic-rcc.org/ 

2.2 Arctic Climate Forum 

One of the important flagship activities of ArcRCC-Network is Arctic Climate Forum (ACF), its first 
session was held in May 2018 Ottawa, Canada. Since then, ACF sessions have been held regularly, 
twice a year (in May and October), bringing together professional communities from the National 
Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) and key stakeholders across the region to discuss 
its impacts in various sectors. The ACF sessions have been regularly producing comprehensive 
consensus statements for the upcoming boreal summer and winter seasons respectively, consisting of 
reviews of climate monitoring information, recent observations and seasonal forecasts based on 
dynamical models. The ACF also serves as a feedback mechanism to identify users’ needs and 
requirement in additional products, and ArcRCC network makes efforts to address these needs to the 
extent possible by continuously expanding the portfolio of its products and services. 

All materials of sessions are available at https://www.arctic-rcc.org/acf. 
The next face-to-face session will be held in May 2025 in Canada.

2.3 Sustaining Arctic Observing Networks (SAON) 

WMO has confirm in 2024 its interest to continue the engagements in the SAON activities and through 
its Committee for Observations and the Arctic Data Committee, as SAON is restarting its activities. 
WMO is represented in these structures by Ms Rodica Nitu (WMO Secretariat) and Dr Øystein Godøy 
(Norway, Lead Cryosphere and Polar Data of the Global Cryosphere Watch). The key contributions 
envisaged are related to extending the experience and practices of the WMO Integrated Global 
Observing Network (WIGOS) and of the WMO Information System (WIS) to support the observations 
and data exchange in support of the Arctic scientific and service goals. An additional contribution is 
possible through the Global Atmosphere Watch (GAW) – see next section. 

2.4 Arctic PASSION - Pan-Arctic Observing System of Systems - Implementing Observations for Societal 
Needs 

WMO has endorsed and is actively engaged in the delivery of results of the Horizon 2020 project Pan-
Arctic Observing System of Systems - Implementing Observations for Societal Needs. A specific 
contribution is made to the Work Package 3, Bringing the Arctic Data System to Action, with support 
provided through the Global Cryosphere Watch of the WMO Infrastructure Commission. 

2.5 Marine Services and engagements with the program on the Protection on the Arctic Marine 
Environment 

WMO has been actively supporting the Arctic METAREA activities through Members States (Norway, 
Canada, Russian Federation) as per IMO instruments, in particular the implementation of Iridium 
SafetyCast Service to enhance polar coverage. 

WMO updated its Sea-ice Information and Services (WMO No. 574) in 2024 to incorporate 
advancements in satellite observation techniques. Additionally, WMO has been developing the S-41X 
Product Specifications in support of E-Navigation, notably the S-411-Dynamic Ice Information standard 
for display in an ECDIS. 

WMO and IMO co-hosted the 2nd WMO-IMO Symposium on Extreme Maritime Weather, London, UK, 
23-26 September 2024. There was a side event on Metocean forecasting support in polar regions. 

WMO has contributed to the Protection of the Arctic Marine Environment (PAME) Shipping Expert 
Group (SEG) meeting in November 2024. 

WMO maintains a web portal to support the Arctic Shipping Best Practice Information Forum, at 
https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/Marine/WMO-Support-for-Shipping-polar-waters 

2.6 Polar Coupled Assimilation and Prediction for Services (PCAPS) 

The Polar Coupled Analysis and Prediction for Services (PCAPS) is one of the new projects of the World 
Weather Research Programme (WWRP) Implementation Plan, (https://www.wwrp-pcaps.net), 
anticipated to run from 2024 to 2028. 

With the overarching goal “to improve the actionability, impact, and fidelity of environmental 
forecasting for human and environmental well-being in the Arctic and Antarctic regions”, PCAPS will 
undertake research that leads to improved service provision for vulnerable communities and those 
operating in the fast-changing polar regions. The focus will be on improving coupled weather and 
climate forecasting models, particularly in predicting small-scale processes essential for accurate 
forecasts in the context of improving overall service provision. PCAPS recognizes the complexity of 
interactions in polar socio-ecological systems and aims to enhance environmental forecasting services 
with diverse user contexts in mind by facilitating the provision of more accurate, reliable, and usable 
prediction services. Emphasizing the integration of social and natural scientific endeavors, along with 
transdisciplinary engagement, PCAPS aims to facilitate the exchange of knowledge at the science-
policy-service-user interface to improve the fidelity, actionability and impact of environmental 
forecasting services. 

It is anticipated that the WMO contribution to the fifth International Polar Year (IPY) (2032-2033) will 
be informed and assisted by the outcomes from PCAPS, among other WMO projects and programmes.

If applicable, please describe in no more than one page your State’s or Organization’s 
future plans for contributing to the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, Task 
Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Please highlight intentions to contribute to specific projects 
and to collaborate with Permanent Participants. 
 

WMO is committed to continue its engagements with SAON, AMAP, and PAME at the technical and 
scientific level. Contributions will be possible through the bi-annual Arctic Climate Forums, the work of 
PHORS, GCW, the Global Atmosphere Watch (GAW), and the World Weather Research Programme 
(WWRP). 

A particular area of engagement is that related to the support for the organization of the 5th International 
Polar Year (IPY) together with the International Arctic Scientific Committee (IASC) and the Scientific 
Committee for Antarctic Research (SCAR). The 79th session of the WMO Executive Council will adopt a 
resolution regarding this support and the call to the WMO Members, for engagement. The engagement 
will be facilitated through PHORS. 

The next face to face meeting of PHORS is tentatively scheduled for February 2026, to be hosted by New 
Zealand. 

 
The United Nations General Assembly Resolution A/RES/77/158 declared 2025 as the International Year of 
Glaciers’ Preservation (IYGP 2025) and designated March 21st as the annual World Day for Glaciers (WGD), 
starting in 2025. This resolution entrusts WMO and UNESCO to co-facilitate the implementation of the 
IYGP and the observance of the WGD, in cooperation with governments, relevant United Nations 
organizations and other stakeholders including organisations engaged in the Artic Council. 

 

Additional contributions to the Sustaining Arctic Observing Networks (SAON) 

Several pollutants, including black carbon and methane, are continuously monitored in Arctic regions by 
atmospheric facilities contributing to the Global Atmosphere Watch (GAW) program of the World 
Meteorological Organization (WMO). Analysis of long-term data records (>10 years) from six facilities 
located in the Arctic and Sub-Arctic regions shows no strong evidence of systematic increasing or 
decreasing trends for absorbing aerosols (Collau Coen et al., 2020). This is despite the fact that the Arctic 
region is changing rapidly, and the impact of evolving transport patterns, atmospheric removal processes, 
or local sources may shift in the future. 

The number and intensity of wildfires are increasing in several Arctic regions, with long-range transport of 
smoke being detected at Arctic GAW stations. This increase in wildfires may counteract the global 
decrease in anthropogenic emissions, as illustrated in the WMO Air Quality and Climate Bulletin #4 (2024). 
How such changes in wildfire emissions lead to observable shifts in trends remains an important area for 
future analyses. 

Greenhouse gases, including methane, are also monitored from 12 facilities located in the Arctic and Sub-
Arctic regions, contributing to the establishment of global concentrations and trends. In 2023, atmospheric 
CH₄ reached a record high of 1934 ± 2 ppb, most likely driven by microbial emissions from wetlands, 
livestock, waste, and rice paddies. Given that Arctic landmasses hold vast stores of carbon, the thawing of 
Arctic permafrost represents another potential climate feedback. However, a large increase in emissions 
from the Arctic has not yet been detected.
